Diversity of macroinvertebrates positively correlates with diversity of macrophytes in karst ponds Igor Zelnik*, Neža Gregorič, Ana Tratnik University of Ljubljana, Biotechnical Faculty, Department of Biology, Jamnikarjeva 101, SI-1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Emergent macrophytes Karst ponds Montane pastures South-eastern calcareous Alps Slovenia ABSTRACT Relations between diversity of macrophytes and macroinvertebrates in 16 karst ponds on the outskirts of SE Alps (Slovenia) were investigated. Inventory of macrophytes was performed and their cover values were estimated. Macroinvertebrates were sampled with hand net. Correlations between environmental factors and parameters of taxonomic richness and diversity of the communities were calculated. Influences of environmental parameters on the structure of communities were analyzed. Results confirmed significant positive correlations between diversity of macrophytes and macroinvertebrates. The most abundant and most species-rich group of plants were emergent macrophytes. Richness and diversity of macrophytes were more important than their coverage for diversity of macroinvertebrates. A negative direct influence of the cattle to macrophytes as well as to macroinvertebrates was calculated. We can conclude that diversity of macrophytes had a positive influence on diversity of macroinvertebrate community. High diversity of emergent macrophytes supports high diversity of macroinvertebrate communities – directly as higher number of hiding places, oviposition sites or food sources and indirectly with more efficient uptake of excessive nutrients. Despite the negative direct influence of the cattle to macrophytes that we calculated, trampling positively influences macrophytes and indirectly also macroinvertebrates in karst ponds, since it enables the existence of these specific waterbodies in the long run. 1. Introduction Ponds are waterbodies shallow enough that light can reach the bottom in the entire ecosystem and enable photosynthesis and high number of ecological niches (Wetzel, 2001). Ponds also fall in the scope of wetlands according to definition by Ramsar convention and amended definition by Gopal (2016), respectively. Unlike the lakes, surface of a pond is lower than 2 hectares (De Meester et al., 2005; Hassall et al., 2011). Despite their small size, ponds have a great biodiversity which is relatively higher than in lakes and watercourses (Williams et al., 2004; Biggs et al., 2005; Davies et al., 2008). Ponds have different ecological functioning than lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2005) also because of their higher perimeter:area ratio which enhances biogeochemical functions (Marton et al., 2015; Cohen et al., 2016), so the rate of nutrient cycling is higher than in lakes (Wetzel, 2001). Ponds in alpine regions have been less studied than lakes (Hamerlik et al., 2014), but their relatively higher diversity emphasizes their relevance for regional diversity in mountain areas (Hamerlik et al., 2014). Since the conservation of freshwaters has fallen behind the conservation of terrestrial ecosystems (Stendera et al., 2012), alpine ponds offer an opportunity to partly fill that gap. 1.1. Karst ponds Karst ponds are small artificial lentic waterbodies made to collect and store rainwater in karstic landscapes where there are no natural surface waterbodies. Their primary role of being a water supply has been accompanied, in last decades, by their significant contribution to biodiversity (Zelnik et al., 2012). Existence, diversity and quality of karst ponds depend on human activities. Activity which is most tightly connected with them is grazing by cattle and in some places horses. Mountain pasture depends on sufficient number of karst ponds containing water of considerable quality which is often difficult to provide. Protection of karst ponds from pollution is possible only with suitable management of ponds and their catchments, respectively. Harrison et al. (2017) report that grazing can alter wetland productivity and diversity by removing or trampling vegetation, compacting soil, increasing erosion, and adding nutrients. 1.2. Communities of macrophytes and macroinvertebrates in ponds Few studies have simultaneously evaluated plant and animal communities in ponds (e.g., Oertli et al., 2002; Nicolet et al., 2004; Landi et al., 2012). Bagella et al. (2010) argue that simultaneous survey of several communities would enable a better understanding of ecosystem functionality. Different aquatic communities respond differently to environmental factors, so biodiversity patterns and factors which determine them cannot be generalized to other communities (Gascón et al., 2009). Macrophytes are an important structural element of aquatic ecosystems and sustain biodiversity (Hassall et al., 2011; Ilg and Oertli, 2014), since they increase number of mesohabitats for invertebrates (Heino, 2000; Robin et al., 2014). Moreover, they are essential for ecosystem functioning and for reaching a good ecological status of aquatic ecosystems. Abundance and diversity of macrophytes depend on water quality, depth and substrate characteristics (Baattrup-Pedersen and Riis, 1999), but they also affect water quality, so they have direct and indirect impacts on diversity of macroinvertebrates. Their preservation requires sufficient knowledge on how plant communities are controlled by environmental factors (Bornette and Puijalon, 2011), but there are still important gaps in such knowledge (Chappuis et al., 2011). Significant positive correlations between diversity of macrophyte and invertebrate communities in ponds has been reported in studies conducted in different European regions like Alpine (Oertli et al., 2002, 2008; Ilg and Oertli 2014), Mediterranean (Della Bella et al., 2008; Bagella et al., 2010) and Atlantic (Nicolet et al., 2004; Hassall et al., 2011). Macrophytes increase heterogeneity of the habitat, providing shelters, living space, oviposition sites and food for macroinvertebrates (Jeppesen et al., 1997; Wetzel, 2001). Environmental factors that drive pond biodiversity are specific to region (Alvarez Cobelas et al., 2005; De Marco et al., 2014) as well as to elevation range (Hindem et al., 2005; Fernández-Alaez, 2017). Based on these findings mountain ponds should be treated differently than lowland ponds and different management plans should be implemented. We hypothesized that i) composition of macrophyte and macroinvertebrate communities will be influenced by different sets of environmental variables characteristic to the region and elevation; ii) that species richness and diversity of macrophytes positively correlates with richness and diversity of macroinvertebrates; iii) while intensity of grazing negatively influences the diversity of both studied communities. 2. Material and methods 2.1. Study area Macrophyte and macroinvertebrate communities as well as selected environmental variables in 16 karst ponds located mostly on karst plateaus were analyzed. Studied ponds were selected using satellite images of pasture landscapes in different parts of SE calcareous Alps that occur in NW and N Slovenia to avoid biased selection in the field. Selected ponds can be found in montane and subalpine belt at altitudes between 1000 and 1800 m a.s.l. in Alpine region of Slovenia, where mountain pastures are widespread and grazed by cattle during the summer. Altitude and coordinates (Gauss-Krüger system) of each pond was obtained with GPS device (Table 1). Data on average annual precipitation was found in Cegnar (2003). Karst ponds were sampled during the summer in the year 2014 from July 1 to September 5, beginning at lower altitudes and ending at the highest sites. The climate is alpine with enough rain during the summer months to maintain permanent ponds despite being used by cattle. 2.2. Macrophyte survey Macrophytes were recorded and their cover values in percentage scale were estimated. Macrophyte were classified in different groups according to Ellenberg’s indicator value (EIV) for humidity of the site (Ellenberg et al., 2001), like submerged or emergent macrophytes or flood-meadow taxa (Table 2). 2.3. Macroinvertebrate survey MI were sampled according to modified PLOCH method described in Oertli et al. (2005), which suggests sampling in two habitats – in land-water interface, which represents the edge of the pond, and the bottom of the pond, which is the central part of the pond. Firstly the assessment of substrata was performed and cover values (in %) of specific substrate categories were estimated. Afterwards from 6 to 8 sampling plots were selected according to the size of the pond to cover both habitats as well as most representative mesohabitats within them. Quantitative sampling of various substrata (mesohabitats) was performed with hand-net 25 × 25 cm, (pores 0.5 × 0.5 mm) from the plot of 25 × 50 cm for 30 s. Samples were fixed and stored for further analyses in laboratory. Determination to the level of family was done with the help of determination keys in Tachet et al. (2010). Abundance of each taxon was expressed as the share of individuals counted in the sample. 2.4. Environmental factors At each sampling pH, water temperature, electric conductivity, oxygen concentration and saturation were measured with multimeter (EUTECH, PCD 650). Turbidity of the water was measured as Secchi depth. Water samples were analyzed in laboratory for concentrations of: TP, PO4^{3-}, NO3-N, NH4-N, TN, as well as TSS and TDS. The cuvette tests HACH Lange were performed for the content of ammonium (LCK 304), nitrate (LCK 339) and phosphate (LCK 349). We measured the concentrations with the spectrophotometer HACH Lange LT 200. Water depth was also measured, as well as the surface parameters (length and width or diameter) which were used for calculation of approximate surface and volume. Types and proportions of inorganic and organic substrate (%) were surveyed according to classification by AQEM (2002). Biotic parameters were also estimated – like cover of the pond surface (%) with tree canopies, abundance (%) of woody species (willows), abundance (%) of filamentous algae. We estimated the share of trampled banks expressed as the percentage of the pond perimeter as well as the intensity of trampling on a six-degree scale: 0 = no signs of trampling; 1 = single hoof-prints, without significant influence on vegetation; 2 = groups of hoof-prints, no major influence on vegetation; 3 = trampled areas with strips of bare ground within remaining strips of vegetation; 4 = intensively trampled areas with only some bunches of remaining vegetation; 5 = completely trampled area, bare ground. Characteristics of the catchment area around each pond were surveyed as the number of habitat types within 10 m as well as 50 m from the water edge. Moreover, land-use intensity within 50 m from the pond was estimated on a five-degree scale: 5 = undisturbed forest (negligible human influence); 4 = mixture of forest and grassland; 3 = extensively grazed pastures, grassland/forest; 2 = extensively grazed pastures; 1 = intensively grazed pastures. 2.5. Diversity indices Richness of macrophytes was expressed as the number of species of: all vascular plants (VP), aquatic macrophytes (AM), emergent macrophytes (EM), submerged macrophytes (SM) and flood-meadow species (Table 2). Diversity or heterogeneity of macrophyte community was calculated as Shannon-Wiener (S-W) diversity index and Margalef I. Zelnik et al. Ecological Engineering 117 (2018) 96–103

Richness of macroinvertebrate community was expressed as number of families determined in the samples and as the number of higher taxa (e.g., order, subclass). Heterogeneity or diversity of macroinvertebrates was calculated as Shannon-Wiener (S-W) diversity index and Margalef (Mrg) diversity index on the base of shares of families as well as higher taxa. For both communities abundances were also determined. In case of macrophytes cover values were used, while in case of macroinvertebrate number of individuals of each taxon in the sample were counted. 2.6. Statistic analyses Relations between diversity indices and structural elements of both communities were calculated using Spearman correlations on ranks, as well as between diversity indices and environmental factors to find direct relations between diversity and specific elements of the communities with environmental factors. The influence of specific environmental factors on the taxonomic composition of studied communities were checked by direct gradient analysis. Firstly, we conducted a detrended correspondence analysis (DCA), which showed linear distribution in case of macroinvertebrates and slow turnover of taxonomic data along potential gradients (gradient length = 1.81 S.D., eigenvalue of 1st axis = 0.214), so we used redundancy analysis (RDA). In case of macrophytes we got different result (gradient length = 3.11 S.D., eigenvalue of 1st axis = 0.559), so we used canonical correspondence analysis (CCA). Analyses were performed with the software package CANOCO 4.5 (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). Both sets of data were log transformed. With RDA and CCA, respectively, we checked the relation between species composition and selected factors, and the share of the variability of the mentioned community they explain. This was conducted with the series of RDAs and CCAs, respectively. The impact of environmental factors on species composition was examined by forward selection of variables, where 499 permutations were applied. We took into account only those who had statistically significant effect (p < 0.05). Ordination diagrams were created on the basis of the results of RDA and CCA, respectively. 3. Results Although the bedrock is more or less the same in all locations, considerable differences of physical and chemical conditions were measured (Table 3). Considering the composition of inorganic substrate, the differences were negligible (Table 4) since clay and silt dominated in all but two ponds. In pond MEN2 there was a plastic foil used instead of the impervious clayish layer, while in pond KR3 sand and gravel formed the bottom. 3.1. Different response of communities to environmental factors The most influential factors determining composition of the macrophyte community were: concentrations of TN (14.3% of TVE) and TP (9.4% of TVE) as well as coverage of the bottom with stony substrate (7.8% of TVE). These three factors significantly influenced the floristic composition of macrophyte community (Fig. 1) and together explained 31.5% of its variability. Ponds on the diagram (Fig. 1) are distributed according to relations between composition of macrophyte species and their distributions along significant gradients. Environmental factors that significantly influenced the composition of macroinvertebrate community were: Land-use in the catchment area (18% of TVE) and minimal measured O₂ saturation of the water (16% of TVE). These two factors together explained 34% of its variability. Ponds on the diagram (Fig. 2) are distributed according to relations between composition of macroinvertebrate families and their distributions along two significant gradients. 3.2. Correlations Correlations between coverage, species richness and diversity of different groups of macrophytes and macroinvertebrates are presented in Table 5. Correlations between richness and diversity of macroinvertebrates and environmental parameters were also calculated to find out direct relations between macroinvertebrates and abiotic factors. There was also negative correlation between diversity of macroinvertebrates and parameters of trophic status (Secchi depth, TP, nitrates). Considering the relations between abundance expressed as total coverage (TC), species richness and diversity of macrophytes and environmental factors (Table 7) the texture of the substrate turned out to be among the most important factors. The share of stony substrate had negatively correlated with diversity, richness and total coverage of AM. Trophic status, expressed as amount of TDS and concentration of NH4-N had negative influence to the species richness and diversity (S-W and Mrg index) of macrophytes. Trampling by cattle negatively correlated with diversity of AM. communities enable better understanding of ecosystem functionality in ponds. Composition of macrophyte communities were significantly influenced by concentrations of TN (14.3% of TVE) and TP (9.4% of TVE) as well as coverage of stony substrate (7.8% of TVE), which together explained 31.5% of the total variability of the vegetation. In first place, composition was driven by nutrient contents. Concentrations of nutrients are reported to have significant influence on macrophytes also by Lumbreiras et al. (2012) and Rosset et al. (2014). Fernández-Aláez et al. (2017) report conductivity and TP (together 59% of TVE) as the most important for macrophyte community composition, whereas nitrogen, which was the most important factor in our case, as not important. The share of stony substrate turned out to be the third most important factor for the variability of macrophyte community. Lacoul and Freedman (2006) also report significant influence of substrate characteristics on the structure of macrophyte community. Composition of macroinvertebrate communities was significantly influenced by land-use in the catchment area (18% of TVE) and minimal O2 saturation of water (16% of TVE), together explaining 34% of variability of the communities. Bird and Day (2016) report that composition of invertebrate community reflects land-use changes. But, these changes caused a rise in pH (Bird and Day 2016), which actually caused the change of macroinvertebrate community. In our case, land-use was most important factor that shaped the composition of macroinvertebrate community, while pH was not important. 4. Discussion 4.1. Different response of macrophyte and macroinvertebrate communities Results revealed totally different sets of environmental factors that influenced studied communities. Factors that significantly influenced the composition of macrophyte communities were concentration of TN, TP and coverage of stony substrate, while composition of macroinvertebrate communities were influenced by land-use in the catchment area and minimal O2 saturation. Similarly, Oertli et al. (2002) and Bagella et al. (2010) report that different taxonomic groups occurring in ponds showed different responses to environmental factors. We agree with Bagella et al. Positive correlations between macrophyte and invertebrate diversity in ponds has been reported from different European regions like: Alpine (Oertli et al., 2002), Mediterranean (Bazzanti et al., 2003; Bagella et al., 2010), and Atlantic (Nicolet et al., 2004). Such importance could be explained also with the conclusions (Burdett and Watts 2009) that vegetation provides trophic resources for invertebrates. Our results revealed that diversity of macrophytes was far more important for diversity of macroinvertebrates than abundance or coverage of macrophytes, although there are positive correlations reported as well (Biggs et al., 2005). The only significant positive correlations regarding this aspect were between cover of EM and mosses and diversity of macroinvertebrate families (Table 5). Moreover, we found that the richness of EM was significantly correlated with richness and diversity of macroinvertebrate community (Table 5). Fernández-Zamudio et al. (2016) also report that the edges of ponds contained a great number of EM which create a complex structure hosting a great number of macroinvertebrates. We found that abundance of Odonata highly correlated with abundance and species richness of EM and AM, respectively. Schindler et al. (2003) report that macrophyte richness influence the composition of dragonfly assemblages in ponds. Diversity of AM is important for larvae of Odonata as a refuge against predators and specific oviposition sites (De Marco et al., 2014). 4.3. Correlations between diversity of macrophyte community and environmental factors Considering the relations between diversity of macrophytes and environmental factors, the share of stony substrate significantly negatively correlated with number of VP, AM and EM, while the share of gravel and sand negatively correlated with diversity of VP and AM (Table 7). The influence of substrate characteristics on aquatic macrophyte richness has been previously reported by Lacoul and Freedman, (2006). The amount of TDS and concentration of NH4-N which mirrored trophic conditions had negative influence to the number of VP, S-W and Mrg index, as well as number of AM. This findings are in accordance with conclusion by Stendera et al. (2012) who argue that eutrophication is among the most important stressors for freshwater biodiversity. Lumbraeras et al. (2016) report that ponds in good status have a higher number of macrophyte species than less preserved. Land-use in the catchment and its changes influence the diversity of macrophyte community (Hill and Keddy 1992; Capers et al., 2010). Species richness and diversity of macrophytes did not negatively correlate with land-use in the catchment, but with the intensity and extent of trampling of the banks, which causes physical disturbance to emergent vegetation and contribute to concentration of nutrients and turbidity, which influence the structure of macrophyte communities (Mitsch and Gosselink 2000). Ponds where such disturbances are very frequent contain vegetation with lower coverage, lower number of communities as well as species (Declerck et al., 2006). On the other hand, light to moderate intensity of grazing and disturbances by cattle can be used to maintain open water in the ponds and to hinder succession with EM, which helps to maintain diverse communities (Marty, 2005). This is also in accordance with Stendera et al. (2012), who report that heterogeneity and disturbance are major drivers of freshwater biodiversity. Despite the common pattern of decreasing species richness with altitude, which is reported by many researchers (e.g. Hrivanák et al., 2013; Chappuis et al., 2011; Kochjarová et al., 2017), our results did not confirm this theory as it was not important for composition nor for diversity. 4.4. Correlations between diversity of macroinvertebrates and environmental parameters Relations between environmental parameters and macroinvertebrates were more complex than with macrophytes, since numerous significant correlations were calculated (Table 6). Our results differed much from those published in Bird and Day (2016) who report that physical and chemical gradients did not correlate with species richness. Surface of the pond and T of the water, which do not reflect the quality of the pond, positively correlated with richness and diversity of macroinvertebrates. Positive correlation between surface area and richness and diversity of macroinvertebrates is in accordance with positive species-area relationship (MacArthur and Wilson, 1967). Moreover, surface area is a direct measure of potential available habitats in waterbodies (Triantis and Sfenthourakis, 2005). This result is interesting, since there was no such relation in case of macrophytes. A positive relationship between invertebrate richness and pond size was also found by Biggs et al. (2005), Studinski and Grubbs (2007), De Marco et al. (2014), whereas Boix et al. (2008), Hamerlik et al. (2014) found no relationship between them. Human pressure expressed as land use in the catchment and intensity of trampling of the banks by cattle negatively correlated with diversity of macroinvertebrates. Overgrazing by cattle causes eutrophication, physical destruction of the vegetation and disturbance (Bouahim et al., 2014), which can result in an impoverishment of the fauna. We also found out that the extent and intensity of trampling of the banks and/or littoral zone negatively correlated with diversity and richness of macroinvertebrates as well as macrophytes. Similarly Morrison and Bohlen (2010) report that intensive grazing lowers diversity and richness of aquatic invertebrates, since it lowers the complexity and biomass of vegetation and increase nutrient levels, which change macrophyte communities used by invertebrates (Steinman et al., 2003). Turbidity and contents of TP and nitrates which represent trophic status, negatively correlated with diversity of MI, meaning that lower quality of pond ecosystem causes a decrease in diversity and richness of its communities. High turbidity inhibits the development of most of the macrophytes (Robin et al., 2014) and lowers the efficiency of numerous visually oriented predacious macro-invertebrates (De Marco et al., 2014), so the richness of both groups is negatively correlated to eutrophication of ponds. 4.5. Conservation of ponds If we want to preserve the biodiversity of ponds, these small waterbodies, should not be treated as self-sufficient, but as parts of the network of habitats (Hassall et al., 2011). Since none of the studied ponds hosted entire community recorded, ponds in alpine region should be considered as patches of fragmented habitat (Alfonso et al., 2016). In general, the legislation on pond conservation is inadequate (Cereghino et al., 2014). Alfonso et al. (2016) point out that Habitat Directive (1992/43/EEC) includes only Mediterranean Temporary Ponds as priority habitats, whereas WFD (2000/60/EEC) refers only to lentic ecosystems larger than 50 ha. Nevertheless, measures have to be taken to prevent further losses. Lower intensity of grazing and buffer zones around ponds should be implemented as soon as possible (Gilbert et al., 2017). Harrison et al. (2017) suggest that reduction in grazing intensity can be achieved also with fencing and seasonal restrictions of grazing. However, light to moderate intensity of grazing is suitable, especially as it helps to hinder the succession with emergent vegetation (Murkin et al., 1997). This is also in accordance with intermediate disturbance hypothesis (Grime, 1973). 5. Conclusions Results of this study confirmed significant positive correlations between diversity of macrophytes and macroinvertebrates, which can be explained as important influence of diversity of macrophytes on diversity of macroinvertebrate community. The most important group of macrophytes for biodiversity of ponds, were EM, which were also most abundant and species-rich group. Diversity of EM supports high diversity of macroinvertebrates directly, with higher number of micro-habitats, hiding places, oviposition sites, food sources, as well as indirectly with more efficient uptake of excessive nutrients. Diversity of macrophytes was far more important for diversity of macroinvertebrates than coverage. Despite the negative direct influence of the cattle to macrophytes that we calculated, trampling positively influences the macrophytes and indirectly also macroinvertebrates in karst ponds, since it enables the existence of these artificial waterbodies in the long run. 5.1. Recommendations for management In restoration of ponds and in creation of new ones we recommend to use clayey or loamy substrate without additional paving or reinforcement of the banks with stones and gravel. New ponds should be of sufficient size, exceeding 100 m². Pasture communities need to be advised to decrease intensity of grazing to achieve better trophic status of the ponds as well as to minimize the pressure to aquifers which are important source of drinking water for population in alpine valleys and basins. Grazing intensity could be reduced with decrease in share of pastures around ponds, as well as with decrease in cattle density (number of animals per area). A measure that we strongly recommend to reduce disturbance of the habitats by trampling and grazing of buffer zone and/or EM is fencing of the part of the pond. This measure would help to reach: a) a better trophic status of the pond which also means better water quality; b) higher biodiversity of macrophyte and consequently macroinvertebrate communities. Acknowledgments The authors thank to Dragan Abram for the assistance in the laboratory and to prof. Mateja Germ for critical revision of the manuscript and useful comments. Funding This work was partly supported by the Ministry of Education, Science and Sport, Republic of Slovenia, through the Program Biology of Plants (Grant number: P1-0212 33135). Conflict of interest None. Appendix A. Supplementary data Supplementary data associated with this article can be found, in the online version, at http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.ecoleng.2018.03.019.

Environmental Conditions and Macrophytes of Karst Ponds Igor Zelnik*, Mateja Potisek, Alenka Gaberščik Department of Biology, Biotechnical Faculty, University of Ljubljana, Večna pot 111, 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia Received: 19 December 2011 Accepted: 13 June 2012 Abstract Man-made karst ponds are the only surface water bodies in the Karst region (SW Slovenia, NE Italy) and support variable biotic communities, depending on ecological parameters and human activities. The aim of our study was to establish the relationship between environmental conditions (land-use of the catchment, vegetation of the banktop zone, morphological properties of the ponds, water quality parameters, the presence of fish) and aquatic macrophyte species composition and abundance. The survey of 28 ponds was performed in the peak vegetation period in 2009. The most abundant emergent macrophytes found were Typha latifolia, Alisma plantago-aquatica, Eleocharis palustris agg., and Alisma lanceolatum, while the most common hydrophytes were Lemna minor, Chara spp., Nymphaea alba, and Potamogeton natans. About 15% of all species found in ponds are included in the “Red” list of endangered plant species of Slovenia. The presence of fish, water transparency, pH, land-use of the pond catchment and quality of shore substrate were detected as the most influential factors determining aquatic macrophyte communities. Keywords: Karst, pond, environmental parameter, floristic composition Introduction Ponds are small lentic ecosystems that permanently or temporarily hold water [1]. They are shallow and their size ranges from a few square metres to several hectares. They can be natural or man-made. Their number is much higher than that of large lakes, which constitute a small percentage of the total number of lakes [2]. Despite this, studies of lentic ecosystems have concentrated mainly on moderately large lakes [2]. Ponds differ functionally from larger lakes [3], since their littoral structure and its productivity dominates the ecosystem [2]. Despite their small size they contain a significant part of aquatic biodiversity on the landscape scale [4, 5]. Humans have created millions of ponds for multiple purposes [2], but today they serve as refugia for a variety of freshwater biota [5] and are, as such, an irreplaceable type of habitat [6-8]. The biotic communities that develop in ponds depend on environmental conditions and human activity. Several studies document clear associations between the communities and a variety of environmental gradients, such as hydro-period [9, 10], surface area [11], and water properties like water transparency, nutrient availability, and pH [12-14]. Compared to rivers and lakes, ponds exhibit greater environmental and, consequently, biotic amplitudes [15]. Macrophytes are important components of aquatic ecosystems (including ponds), affecting their function through energy flow, nutrient cycling, sedimentation processes, and habitat provision [16, 17]. Their presence and abundance reflect the quality of the ecosystem as a whole. Aquatic macrophytes not only are affected by water quality, but they also affect water quality and provide food and refugia for aquatic invertebrates and fish [11, 18, 19]. Their growth is controlled by a variety of factors, namely water quality, water depth, water movement, substrate characteristics, and biotic interactions [20, 21]. Therefore, a survey of aquatic macrophytes is important from the point of 1912 Zelnik I., et al. view of plant species diversity, as well as of factors explaining the diversity of other groups (e.g. macro-invertebrates, periphyton) [22] and as indicators of water and habitat quality [e.g. 23-28]. Deterioration of the physical environment and eutrophication of water bodies result in changes in macrophyte distribution, a decline in aquatic macrophyte species richness, and a greater abundance of more resistant species [29]. Karst ponds are of human origin, presenting an outstanding natural and cultural heritage [30]. Following mass regulation of rivers and streams all over Europe, man-made systems have become a substitute habitat for numerous organisms [6]. This is the case in the karst ponds, which provide an important network of water-bodies in the Karst Region. The fact, that they are the only surface water-bodies on the Karst Plateau [31] makes them even more important. The aims of our study were to examine the habitat characteristics and/or ecological conditions in karst ponds, as well as surveying the presence and abundance of aquatic macrophyte species. We also aimed to establish the relations between habitat characteristics and aquatic macrophyte species composition. The specific questions addressed were: • Which environmental conditions significantly influence aquatic macrophyte species composition in karst ponds? • How much of the variation of aquatic macrophyte species composition is explained by considered environmental conditions and how do they affect macrophytes species richness? Materials and Methods Study Area Twenty-eight karst ponds were investigated in the Karst region in SW Slovenia. The ponds are distributed on the Karst Plateau along the border with Italy (from 13°38’08” E, 45°50’43” N to 13°59’36” E, 45°39’54” N) (Table 1). The climate is sub-Mediterranean, annual precipitation is 1,500 mm [32] (about two-fold higher than evapotranspiration). The largest amount of precipitation occurs in November, and the least in the peak of the vegetation period in July [32]. The mean annual temperature is 11°C [33]. The altitude ranges from 195 to 420 m a.s.l. Aquatic Macrophyte Survey The abundance of aquatic macrophytes was evaluated using a 5-degree estimation scale [34]: 1 = very rare 2 = infrequent 3 = common 4 = frequent 5 = abundant, predominant The whole pond was a sampling unit. Plants were identified using the following keys: Martinčič et al. [35] and Preston [36]. Plants whose reproductive organs were not present at the time of sampling are listed by genus (e.g. Bidens, Epilobium, Sparganium). The survey was performed in July and August in 2009. The nomenclature of ferns and flowering plants follows Martinčič et al. [35]. The definition of aquatic macrophytes is in accordance with Hutchinson [37] and Wetzel [2], therefore woody species and other non-hygrophilous species were excluded from analyses. Plant species richness in the ponds was calculated as species number (N) per surface area and/or approximate volume of the studied water bodies.

 Environmental Conditions and Macrophytes... 1913 Assessment of Environmental Conditions Parameters were recorded in the field, measured and/or calculated in the laboratory (Table 2). Independent environmental variables were tested for their significance in shaping aquatic macrophyte species composition. These variables can be classified into three groups [38]: quantitative variables, semiquantitative estimates, and categorical variables. Quantitative variables include morphometric parameters of the specific pond (length, width or diameter (m), surface (m²), depth (m), approximate volume (m³), surface:depth ratio (S/d)), and water quality parameters (pH, temperature (T), conductivity (EC), O₂ concentration, O₂ saturation, transparency, chlorophyll-a). Semiquantitative estimates include habitat characteristics (land-use of the catchment, bottom substrate, shore substrate, type of vegetation in banktop zone, width of woody and/or wetland banktop zone). Categorical variables include data about the presence/absence of: fish, filamentous algae, slime, woody species in the pond. Water samples were taken from each pond in August 2009. The majority of the water quality parameters (pH, O₂ concentration, O₂ saturation, T and EC of water) were measured in situ using the portable multi-meter PCD 650 (Eutech Instruments, Singapore). Water transparency and concentration of chlorophyll-a were analyzed spectrophotometrically in the laboratory on the same day. Habitat characteristics were assessed as semiquantitative estimates in a similar way as in many studies of aquatic ecosystems [39-41]. The estimated gradients were as follows: (1) land-use of the pond catchment, according to decreasing human influence (1 = settlement or arable land/vineyard or road, 2 = mixed arable land and grassland, 3 = grassland, 4 = mixed grassland and forest, 5 = forest) (2) the type and/or structure of the shore substrate, according to decreasing coarseness of the substrate (1 = concrete, 2 = stone-wall, 3 = stones and stone-wall, 4 = stones, 5 = loam and clay) (3) of the bottom (1 = concrete, 2 = stones and concrete, 3 = stones, 4 = stones and loam, 5 = loam and clay) (4) width of the littoral zone (1 = <1 m, 2 = 1-5 m, 3 = >5 m) (5) vegetation of the banktop zone, according to decreasing human influence (1 = absent, 2 = ruderals, 3 = perennial herbs and grasses, 4 = pioneer woody species (Salix sp., Populus sp.), 5 = climax species of trees and shrubs). Statistical Analyses Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) was used for exploratory data analysis. The eigenvalue for the first DCA axis was greater than 0.4 and indicated strong unimodality [42], therefore canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) was chosen. Relationships between site conditions and vegetation were analyzed using direct gradient analysis (CCA). Separate CCAs for each environmental variable were performed to test the significance of its influence and the explanation of species composition variation. Forward selection of explanatory variables was used to provide a ranking of the relative importance of the specific variables and to avoid co-linearity [43]. We used the unrestricted Monte Carlo test with 999 permutations to test the statistical significance of the variables and canonical axes. Another CCA was done with a subset of selected variables only (p<0.1), and the proportions of variance explained by these variables were calculated. Some of the variables were not normally distributed so the data were log transformed. Ordination of the ponds according to the most important environmental parameters was made using CCA. The whole set of analyses was performed using CANOCO 4.5 [44]. Differences in environmental parameters between ponds with and without macrophytes were tested for significance using t-test. Species richness was correlated with environmental parameters using Spearman coefficient in SPSS version 17. Results Aquatic Macrophyte Survey Different growth forms of plants were found: submerged hydrophytes, floating hydrophytes, helophytes, marsh species, and flood-meadow species (Table 3). The most abundant aquatic macrophyte species found in karst ponds were: Typha latifolia, Lemna minor, Alisma plantago-aquatica, Eleocharis palustris, Chara spp., Alisma lanceolatum, and Potamogeton natans. Species from the Red List of Slovenia [45] are relatively numerous, constituting 15% of the total of 50 plant species recorded in ponds. Floristically Defined Types of Karst Ponds Leaving aside the smaller group of ponds that contained no aquatic macrophytes, the ordination plot based on results of preliminary DCA showed clustering of the ponds according to floristic composition. Two groups of ponds that were ecologically sound were delineated – a group of seven less similar species-poorer, mostly walled ponds, and the larger group of 15 species-richer ponds with loamy shores. The group of walled ponds was species-poorer and characterized by the presence of different pond-weeds (Potamogeton crispus, P. nodosus, P. natans, P. trichoides) and a higher proportion of other submerged and/or floating hydrophytes, which constitute half of the species. The group of relatively shallow ponds was characterized by a significantly higher total number of plant taxa, with Typha latifolia, Alisma lanceolata, Eleocharis palustris agg., Juncus inflexus, J. effusus, and other emergent macrophytes and marsh species. Emergent species constitute a quarter of all species, hydrophytes only 12%, and marsh species were most common, constituting 36% of the plant taxa. Environmental Conditions and Gradients A preliminary DCA revealed a first gradient length of 6.49 SD, which indicates strong unimodality, so CCA was chosen. Separate CCAs for each environmental variable revealed that some of the variables influence floristic composition significantly: fish presence, water transparency, pH, land-use of the catchment, and shore substrate. Analysis with forward selection provided a ranking of the relative importance of the specific significant variables (Table 4). The presence of fish, water transparency, pH, land-use of the catchment area of the pond, and shore substrate were revealed to be the most influential factors determining aquatic macrophyte communities, explaining species variation significantly. These variables explain 32% of the total variation of the data set. ![Ordination diagrams of karst ponds based on Canonical Correspondence analysis (CCA), with most important environmental variables.](page_320_670_1408_1042.png) Fig. 1. The differences were most significant in the case of shore substrate (p < 0.05), which was concrete, or a stone wall in the first case and mostly loamy, or a mixture of stones and loam, in the latter. Discussion Floristic Gradients and Environmental Parameters The variation of floristic composition is best explained by the following environmental variables: fish presence/absence, water transparency, pH, land-use of the catchment of the pond, and substrate of the shore. Mentioned parameters explained 32% of the variance in plant species composition that was similar to the results obtained for aquatic macrophytes in karstic watercourses in western Slovenia [46], where a similar set of the studied variables explain 28% of the variation. Capers et al. [13] obtained a similar result (27%), while the results by McElarney et al. [47] revealed higher value (56%). The unexplained variation may also be explained by sampling errors, other non-measured parameters, and by the fact that the species-specific recruitment from the soil seed bank and its persistence has a significant impact on the structure and maintenance of the plant-species diversity in wet habitats [48]. Floristic composition was most strongly correlated by fish-presence (7.9% of total variance was explained by this parameter) which, in contrast, had no influence on species richness or the presence of Red List species. A strong role of fish was also found in the study of peri-urban eutrophic ponds by De Backer et al. [14]. Water transparency explained 6.6% of species variance, in accordance with studies showing the importance of submerged macrophytes in maintaining the clear-water state [14, 49, 50]. The amount of phytoplankton, measured as the concentration of chlorophyll-a, was very variable and did not significantly affect plant species composition or abundance, as was shown by Bakker et al. [51]. The number of plant taxa found in 28 karst ponds was 50, which was high compared to the 53 plant taxa found in 9 streams flowing through the agricultural landscape of Eastern Slovenia, and were considered to support rich aquatic macrophyte communities [52]. The percentage of Red List species was relatively high (15%) and similar to results published by Chappuis et al. [53]. Table 4. Canonical Correspondence analysis statistics of 22 karstic ponds. CCA with these five variables (Table 4) was performed, allowing the distribution of the ponds according to floristic composition along the most important environmental gradients to be shown in an ordination diagram (Fig. 1). Ponds with prevailing hydrophytes are distributed on the upper-right side of the diagram in the direction of fish presence (and transparency), which indicates oxic conditions throughout the year in the permanent water phase. Hypoxic conditions normally occur in ponds with a strong input of allochthonous leaf litter in autumn. Species-rich ponds with abundant emergent and marsh species are distributed in the lower-left part of the diagram in the direction of finer shore substrate, enabling the growth of the mentioned species. Arrows representing water transparency and land-use indicate relative correlation that was expected, since the higher proportion of forest or permanent grassland in the catchment area of a pond would result in clearer water. Species number was significantly correlated with surface/depth ratio, shore substrate, surface area of the pond and width of littoral zone (Table 5). The ponds with loamy shores and/or wider littoral zone were not only richer in total species number, but also harboured more Red list species, which were also more abundant. Environmental Factors in Different Pond Types The main differences in environmental conditions between ponds without macrophytes and those with more or less abundant macrophytes, are the type of shore-substrate (p = 0.014) and of bottom-substrate (p = 0.099), as well as the pH of the water (p = 0.078). The mean recorded pH value in ponds without macrophytes was 7.2, while in ponds with plants it was 6.7. The differences were most significant in the case of shore substrate (p < 0.05), which was concrete, or a stone wall in the first case and mostly loamy, or a mixture of stones and loam, in the latter. **p < 0.01, * = p < 0.05, n.s. = not significant Some studies relate the ratio of submerged to emerged macrophyte species with the level of eutrophication [51]. In our study the abundance of helophytes prevailed over that of submerged species. This was not necessarily the consequence of nutrient availability since, in many case, this parameter does not function as a primary factor shaping the aquatic macrophyte community; other factors affecting ecological conditions, such as water depth and fluctuation, could be of greater importance [54]. However, if we take into account the aquatic macrophyte indicator values for ponds proposed by Sager and Lachavanne [27], the surveyed ponds were shown to host species indicating a mesotrophic as well as a mesotrophic to eutrophic state. Water pH was expected to have a significant influence on aquatic macrophyte assemblages, as indicated by a study of alpine ponds [12]. Land-use practices may affect pond characteristics [5, 13, 15, 55, 56], and these changes of the pond environment (e.g. water/sediment quality) may affect aquatic organisms, their species richness, and abundance. Dodson [56] also concluded that land-use was a good predictor of pond biodiversity. In our study, land-use of the catchment of the pond was not significantly correlated with species-richness, but with species composition. Differences in Environmental Factors between Pond Types As expected, the type of shore substrate provided the most significant difference between ponds with and without macrophytes. The semi-natural types of shore, with finely textured substrate (clay, silt and/or loam), were suitable sites (microhabitats) for emergent macrophytes, while in the case of concrete or stony shores, rooted aquatic macrophytes were scarce. The difference in pH between ponds with macrophytes and “empty” ponds also was evident (p = 0.078). The higher pH of the water in non-colonizd ponds could be due to the contribution of Ca-rich concrete and/or stony substrate. Species number did not correlate with depth, but was significantly correlated with size/depth ratio and surface. In the case of alpine lakes [12] depth did not affect biodiversity, while a significant influence of pond size on the aquatic macrophyte community was shown by Bagella et al. [57], who studied Mediterranean temporary ponds. They also established the important role of disturbances. The main disturbances in the ponds studied here are water level fluctuations, since the conditions of ponds in the Karst region depends directly on precipitation [30], which is unequally distributed over the year [32]. In many cases disturbances also could be the consequence of the land-use in the surroundings of the ponds, i.e. trampling, erosion, and invasive species [50]. In our survey invasive alien plant species were not detected in the ponds and were not abundant in the littoral zone. The most abundant species was the invasive tree species Robinia pseudacacia, which is widespread in the Karst region and is important from the point of nitrogen enrichment of ponds [58]. The ponds with more suitable measures (e.g. loamy shores, wider littoral zone) were not only richer in total species number, but also harbored more Red list species, which also were more abundant. To mitigate adverse effects on plant communities, Akasaka et al. [50] suggests that management should focus on the creation of buffer zones. Conclusions Understanding the environmental conditions that maintain high aquatic macrophyte species richness in karst ponds, together with the main disturbances threatening them, is crucial for the conservation of this important heritage. Land-use in the catchment area and the presence of fish-influenced plant species composition. Concrete shores and bottoms, as well as stony walls, prevented the development of complex aquatic macrophyte communities and the increase of species richness. We conclude that reinforcement of the shores with concrete is the main reason for species impoverishment in karst ponds. On the other hand, some species (Potamogeton crispus, P. nodosus) were found only in walled ponds and that contributes to gamma diversity. As was established for alpine lakes [12], karst ponds need a special approach due to the particular water regime in the Karst area. The present findings should be considered in restoration projects, in order to preserve diversity at all levels. Acknowledgements We thank Prof. Roger Pain for correction of the language. We also thank Dragan Abram for his technical assistance in the field and in the laboratory. We are grateful for critical comments and suggestions of the reviewer that helped to improve the quality of the paper.

The resulting transformations removed both objections, and enabled the fitting of the linear regression lines of yield on area shown in Figure 1. The formula for each regression is: Total population: \( \log y = (2.4294 - .4001 \log x) \) Annual sport yield: \( \log y = (1.8692 - .3884 \log x) \) Annual commercial yield: \( \log y = (3.0355 - .3906 \log x) \) ![Graph showing annual yield of gamefish per acre of water surface for lakes from 30 to 50,000 acres in area](page_324_670_1207_1012.png) Figure 2. Calculated curves of the annual sport fishery (gamefish) yield in pounds per acre of water surface for lakes from 30 to 50,000 acres in area. [These curves are derived from the antilogarithms of the regression of annual sport yield on lake area shown in figure 1.] The standard error of estimate was calculated for each regression, and appears (dotted lines) for each regression line in Figure 1. It will be noted that all three measures of fish production show the same rate of decline with increasing size of lake. These data are given in Table II. No attempt has been made to extrapolate the yields for lakes outside the range of sizes available for each type of data. The annual yield of game fish is also shown in Figure 2 in such form that it may be conveniently and quickly estimated for lakes of any size from 30 to 50,000 acres in area. The most obvious characteristic of the yields is the rapid decline in production per acre as the lakes increase in size. The optimistic production estimates of most fishery experts are not borne out; but it is believed that this is owing largely to the fact that such opinions have been based on the production of very small ponds. For instance, the total population falls from 268.5 pounds in ponds of one acre to only 32.3 pounds in lakes of 200 acres. In the range of lakes for which total populations are available, i.e., 1 to 200 acres, the annual yield of sport fish varies from 74.0 to 9.46 pounds per acre, or 27.6 to 29.3 per cent of the total population estimate. As the total populations include fish of all sizes, as well as forage and rough fishes not contained in the gamefish catch, it is obvious that the sportsmen annually harvest a very appreciable proportion of the available gamefish of legal size. In many of the lakes analyzed, even the surprisingly low yields shown could not be sustained in the face of intensive fishing. The commercial catch per acre is much higher than the sport catch in lakes of 10,000 to 50,000 acres. Thus, at 50,000 acres, the sport catch was only 1.11 pounds per acre compared with a commercial catch of 15.85 pounds. This is owing to several causes. First, sport fisheries are carried on in all lakes, while commercial fisheries are confined to selected lakes of higher than average productivity. Second, the commercial fisheries take many rough fishes and pelagic fishes such as lake herring which are not taken by sportsmen. Third, the commercial fisheries usually impose higher fishing intensities. The yield per acre of lake is probably correlated with the relative area of fertile shallow water, which is generally much less in proportion to total area in the larger lakes than in the smaller ones, as indicated by the difference in length of shoreline. Thus, a circular lake of 503 acres has a shoreline of 3.14 miles, or 0.00624 miles per acre, while one of 50,200 acres has a shoreline of only 31.42 miles, or 0.000626 miles per acre, or about one-tenth as much shoreline per acre. Obviously, the shallow, fertile areas usually are relatively much less extensive in the larger lakes. There are various reasons for variation in the yield of lakes of similar size. Some of these differences are related to the physical and chemical conditions of the lake itself, such as depth, temperature, heat budget, and the quantities of various nutrient materials available. Others relate to the populations of fish and other organisms present. Even in lakes which are comparable both physically and chemically, the yield may differ considerably because of a difference in the species present. Making allowances for physical and chemical characteristics, and for annual variations in climatic conditions, the yield of a lake depends in large measure on the natural balance of the populations within the lake. Only occasionally will a lake be producing at its maximum potential capacity. As an illustration, I have drawn upon data given by Foerster (1944) and by Ricker (1937) for Cultus Lake, British Columbia. Foerster gives the number and weight of the young sockeye salmon migrating out of Cultus Lake each year during a 12-year period. (See Table III.) The balance that had obtained during the first nine years of this period was upset during the last three by the extensive removal of species preying on and competing with the sockeye. 36 COPEIA 1946, No. 1 April 30 The data of Table III and the curves in Figure 3 show some interesting relationships. At low levels of abundance (under one million) the relation between the number of sockeye and their total weight appears to be linear. This indicates that at these levels the young sockeye were not competing with one another for food, so that the size of the individuals depended on conditions other than competition. Because, then, of natural limits to the growth potential of the individual, the maximum productivity of the lake was not reached with these small populations (Area A, Figure 3). In the absence of competition, increasing size of population was accompanied by increasing total weight of fish produced. At what point competition began to be a limiting factor is not shown by the data, but at higher levels of abundance (in 1933 and 1929) the growth rate of the individual sockeye was greatly diminished. The maximum productivity can be reached, therefore, only when sockeye are neither too few nor too numerous. Curve 1 shows the probable production in kilograms under natural conditions; the dotted portion was empirically determined. Curve 2 shows the line of approximate maximum production under natural conditions. Curve 3 shows the indicated production for the three years in which the predators and competing species were suppressed. Area A shows the weight lost from the maximum natural production caused chiefly by a population insufficient to utilize the total food supply. Area B shows the weight lost from the maximum natural production when too large a population is present. The suggested cause is the larger amount of food used to sustain life without growth and actual impairment of the food supply owing to the large numbers of fish per unit area.] These curves of production in natural lakes are at present the only guide for predicting the fish production in proposed reservoirs. A reservoir usually differs in certain important features from a natural lake. It is more subject to frequent and severe fluctuations in water level. It is more apt to have the bottom covered with layers of silt. The deep water usually is confined to one end, causing unnatural temperature stratifications. All of these features tend to make the reservoir less productive than the natural lake. Because of the large quantities of organic matter present when first flooded, reservoirs may show a high initial productivity which will be reduced within a short space of years when they have begun to approach as close to a state of equilibrium as a reservoir is likely to attain. Because the productive capacity of a reservoir must be estimated over a long period of years rather than in the short period immediately following construction when production may be high, it follows that the estimate of yield, based on the analysis of yields of natural lakes, will tend to be too high rather than too low. Nevertheless, it seems desirable that pending detailed studies, these data be used to estimate the productivity of proposed reservoirs. How much adjustment in predicted yield needs to be made for the limiting factors discussed above will remain a matter of opinion until adequate studies of these problems have been made. Physical-chemical influences on vernal zooplankton community structure in small lakes and wetlands of Wisconsin, U.S.A.

Jeffrey M. Schell1, Carlos J. Santos-Flores1, Paula E. Allen1, Brian M. Hunker1, Scott Kloehn1, Aaron Michelson1, Richard A. Lillie2 & Stanley I. Dodson1,*
1Department of Zoology, University of Wisconsin, Birge Hall, 430 Lincoln Dr., Madison, WI 53706, U.S.A.
Tel: +608-262-6395. Fax: +608-265-6320. E-mail:sidodson@facstaff.wisc.edu
2Bureau of Integrated Science Services, Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, 1350 Femrite Drive, Monona, WI 53716, U.S.A.
(*Author for correspondence)

Received 24 January 2000; in revised form 9 November 2000; accepted 4 December 2000

Key words: biogeography, zooplankton, lakes, wetlands, Wisconsin, limnology

Abstract

We sampled zooplankton communities from 54 small water bodies distributed throughout Wisconsin to evaluate whether a ‘snap-shot’ of zooplankton community structure during early spring could be used for the purpose of differentiating lakes from wetlands. We collected a single set of zooplankton and water chemistry data during a one-month time window (synchronized from south to north across the state) from an open water site in each basin as a means to minimize and standardize sampling effort and to minimize cascading effects arising from predator–prey interactions with resident and immigrant aquatic insect communities. We identified 53 taxa of zooplankton from 54 sites sampled across Wisconsin. There was an average of 6.83 taxa per site. The zooplankton species were distributed with a great deal of independence. We did not detect significant correlations between number of taxa and geographic region or waterbody size. There was a significant inverse correlation between number of taxa and the concentration of calcium ion, alkalinity and conductivity. One pair of taxa, Lynceus brachyurus and Chaoborus americanus, showed a significant difference in average duration of sites of their respective occurrence. All other pairs of taxa had no significant difference in average latitude, waterbody surface area, total phosphorus, total Kjeldahl nitrogen, alkalinity, conductivity, calcium ion, sulfate, nitrate, silicate or chloride. Taxa were distributed at random among the sites – there were no statistically significant pairs of taxa occurring together or avoiding each other. Multivariate analysis of zooplankton associations showed no evidence of distinct associations that could be used to distinguish lakes from wetlands. Zooplankton community structure appears to be a poor tool for distinguishing between lakes and wetlands, especially at the relatively large scale of Wisconsin (dimension of about 500 km). The data suggest that a small body of water in Wisconsin could be classified as a wetland if it persists in the spring and summer for only about 4 months, and if it is inhabited by Lynceus brachyurus, Eubranchipus bundyi, and if Chaoborus americanus and Chydorus brevilabris are absent.

Introduction

What is a lake? This question is of particular interest in Wisconsin, where lakes are afforded greater legal protection than are wetlands. Ramifications of the designation of a water body or basin depression as a lake or wetland include ownership of the land beneath the water (the state owns lake beds but not wetlands) and application of county zoning ordinances (many use restrictions apply to lakes but not to wetlands). The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (WDNR) has considerable management responsibility for lakes, but less for wetlands. However, the law is vague on the distinction between lakes and wetlands, leading to

</page>

<page number="1">

confusion concerning management of small temporary ponds and marshes (Cowardin et al., 1979; WDNR, 1993).

Historically, the WDNR generally has used a combination of primarily physical attributes to differentiate lakes from wetlands (Cowardin et al., 1979; Semeniuk and Semeniuk, 1995). The list of attributes used to classify a basin included water body size, water depth (e.g. 2 m), location in a topographic depression, water permanence and the presence or absence of a bed, a bank, ordinary high water mark and/or ‘navigability’. Soil and plant community attributes are used in wetland delineation (wetland versus terrestrial boundaries), but neither attribute has been used independently from the above physical characteristics to separate lakes from wetlands.

The wetland-versus-lake issue is difficult to address because the physical differences between the two represent a continuum, and a very dynamic one at that. Small, land-locked, palustrine depressions typically experience dynamic fluctuations in water duration or hydroperiod from one year to another. Resident fauna mostly are adapted to periodic drought (via various life history traits) or are highly mobile and emigrate to nearby permanent water during dry phases or immigrate (recolonize) during subsequent return of standing water (Dodson & Frey, 1991). Among the various animal inhabitants found in these depression basins are numerous microscopic zooplankton. Zooplankton are less mobile than most other invertebrates (e.g. many aquatic insects) and, consequently, they live or die as dictated by the various environmental conditions they encounter. Because water permanence is critical to so many forms of aquatic life forms, the shift between lake (permanent water) and wetland (periodic drying) could cause a dramatic impact on the biota in any particular basin. Well known shifts occur in the presence/absence of various vertebrate and invertebrate predators along the water duration continuum, and these shifts are reflected in changes in invertebrate community structure. Zooplankton are an important component of the food web chain (both as predators and prey) and thus zooplankton community structure is expected to exhibit a response to changes in water duration. Zooplankton serve as potential indicators of past condition as they integrate impacts that cascade through the food web to themselves.

The intent of this paper is (1) to determine whether changes in zooplankton community structure are related to water duration, and (2) if changes in zooplankton community structure do correspond to water duration, can zooplankton community structure be used as a predictive tool to differentiate lakes from wetlands?

In order to distinguish between lakes and wetlands, the WDNR sampled 54 small bodies of water in the Spring of 1996, collecting standard limnological data, and conducting a survey of several biological communities, including aquatic macrophytes, diatoms, aquatic insects and zooplankton. The purpose of this paper is to interpret patterns of distribution of zooplankton, in order to learn whether wetlands can be distinguished from lakes using distribution patterns or associations of zooplankton species.

Early studies on the zooplankton of Wisconsin (U.S.A.) lakes (Birge, 1892; Marsh, 1893; Juday, 1915; Birge & Juday, 1922) recognized that some species were widely distributed along a broad range of conditions, while some crustacean species were restricted to specific habitats or lake-types. The conditions that determine the suitability of a water body, and ultimately dictate the species composition of zooplankton, result from the interplay between geographic, physical, chemical, and biological factors (Brooks & Dodson, 1965, MacArthur & Wilson, 1967; Hutchinson, 1967; Tessier & Horwitz, 1990; Arnott & Vanni, 1993; Lampert & Sommer, 1997; Jenkins & Buikema, 1998).

Geographic location of a basin and its watershed will generally determine its physical environment: water chemistry, climate, etc., (Hutchinson, 1967) and exposure to dispersal vectors, such as waterfowl. Wisconsin can be divided into several geographic units (Finley, 1975). Much of the northern third of the state has crystalline bedrock, contributing to the predominance of oligotrophic lakes. The rest of the state has calcareous sandstone and dolomite bedrock, which generally produces more eutrophic lakes. The western part of the state is adjacent to a major waterfowl migration route, which might have a strong effect on zooplankton distribution relative to the central regions of the state. Wisconsin is divided diagonally into two roughly equal parts by climatic factors, which affect plant distributions (Curtis, 1959). The narrow band of greatest change in plant diversity is called the ‘tension zone’.

In order to answer our fundamental question about whether zooplankton can be used to distinguish wetlands from lakes, it was first necessary to look for effects of geography and water chemistry on the distribution patterns of taxa. If different taxa occur in different parts of the state, then different criteria are needed for the various geographic regions. Any af-

</page>

<page number="2">

fect of water chemistry on species distribution patterns would have to be taken into account when choosing criteria.

Once the effects of geography and water chemistry are accounted for, it is possible to look for patterns of species association that could be used as a criterion for distinguishing wetlands from lakes. Two related characteristics of water bodies are potentially correlated with zooplankton richness or distribution patterns: basin size and duration of liquid surface water (smallest bodies of water tend to dry up each summer and freeze solid during the winter).

Zooplankton species richness (number of species) is directly related to basin size (Dodson, 1992) over a wide range (at least several orders of magnitude) of surface area. We examined basin size and zooplankton species richness for evidence of a break in the relationship that could be used as a criterion for distinguishing wetlands from lakes.

Some of the sites sampled were spring snowmelt depressions containing water for only one or two months. Several others were essentially permanent with standing water present throughout the entire ice-free season. The remainder of the sampled basins were of intermediate water duration. A break in zooplankton associations along this duration continuum could be used as a criterion for the distinction between wetlands and lakes. For example, zooplankton are adapted for living in either temporary or permanent water (Hairston, 1996; Beaver et al., 1999). The cyclopoid copepods Tropocyclops prasinus, Cyclops spp. and Eucyclops agilis and the cladocerans Ceriodaphnia spp. and Scapholeobris mucronata were most common in temporary habitats while calanoid copepods were distinctly absent (Beaver et al., 1999). Other species, such as Aglaodiaptomus leptopus, are generally restricted to permanent ponds that are free of fish.

Materials and methods

Fifty-four ponds and wetlands were selected to represent a wide range in water duration (months of standing water during the ice-free period) from very short to permanent. Most were water bodies for which we had some long-term records (staff gage readings or personal observations) so as to assign an estimated average water duration. Ponds and wetlands were distributed statewide (Fig. 1) to enable us to account for geographic variations in possible indicator taxa. All sampling was completed within a one month time period (April 24–May 23, 1996) beginning in the South and finishing in the North. The narrow time window and sampling strategy employed was intended to minimize possibly confounding influences of temperature and light regimes and cascading biotic interactions on the community structure. Sampling in early Spring specifically was chosen over other periods because it represented the most stable circumstances for the aquatic insect community (sampled concurrently with zooplankton and topic of a separate paper), which was susceptible to rapid fluctuations due to immigration-emigration. We sampled in April–May so that the bitoa present in any particular wetland basin would represent the conditions that occurred during the previous year. The year 1993 was a very wet year and 1994–95 were fairly average.

We collected a single grab water sample from a central basin location using sample containers provided by the State Laboratory of Hygiene (SLH), Madison, WI. We conducted water sampling on the same date (just prior to) as microinvertebrate sampling to minimize effects of seasonal changes on water chemistry. Nutrient samples were preserved with sulfuric acid and dissolved calcium samples were preserved with nitric acid immediately upon collection. Analyses for Ca^{+2}, SO_4^{--2}, Cl^-, total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN), total phosphorus (TP) and Si (all in mg/l) were conducted according to agency protocols (Standard Methods per APHA, 1992).

We collected zooplankton using a plankton net (15 cm diameter opening) equipped with #10 mesh size or 120 \( \mu \)m netting). The selection of a relatively large mesh size was a necessary compromise to minimize clogging of the net due to the excessive amount of fine, particulate, suspended, organic materials present in many of the wetlands in the study. Naturally, we missed many of the smaller members of the zooplankton community, including many rotifers, as a result of using the coarser mesh net. We employed a standardized sampling strategy to collect 3 net sweeps from each basin. Each net sweep consisted of a 2 m horizontal tow, collected by tossing and retrieving the net in a central, open water area within each water basin. In some instances when the water was too shallow to permit a standard tow to be completed, the opening of the net was held vertically while being hand-swept the 2 m tow distance. The contents of one set of 3 tows or sweeps on one date represented the community for each basin. Contents of the net sweeps were transferred to storage containers and preserved in 4% formalin. Samples were delivered to the Department of Zoology, UW-Madison for species analysis. Statistical analysis

All geographic and chemical data were analyzed for pair-wise correlations. We produced a matrix of pair-wise correlation coefficients using simple linear correlation analysis.

Geographic region and number of taxa

The aquatic sites fall into three clusters (Fig. 1): one cluster (Northwestern) at the northwestern end of the tension zone in Wisconsin, near the Mississippi River (a major route for migrating waterfowl); a cluster (North Central) north of the tension zone in the north central highlands; and a cluster (South Central) mostly south of the tension zone in the glaciated tills in the south-central part of the state. Presence or absence of each species was analyzed for pairs of the three regions, using a Chi-square test of independence. The null hypothesis is that a taxon has the same distribution of present and absent observations, regardless of geographic region. We compared twelve taxa that were common enough (occurred at 10 or more sites) to meet standard requirements of the Chi-square test (rarer species have too few occurrences to have the possibility of producing a significant result). Results of these tests were corrected using the Bonferroni method – there were 12 species and 3 comparisons per species, giving a total of 36 comparisons.

Physical and chemical variables and number of taxa

The number of taxa per pond was correlated with latitude, log_{10} surface area in m^2, log_{10}[Ca^{+2}], log_{10} conductivity, pH, alkalinity, log_{10}[Cl^-], log_{10}[SO_4^{--2}], log_{10}TKN, log_{10}TP and log_{10}[Si]). We used multiple Minitab® linear regression. A Backward Elimination (B.E.) and Forward Selection (F.S.) procedure were used with \( t < 2.00 \) or \( t > 2.00 \) used as the elimination or selection criteria, respectively. Simple linear regression models were also run for all parameters and species richness. Significant simple linear regression models were graphed and the least squares trend line was fit to the data.

Physical and chemical variables and distribution of taxa

To determine if species occurrence was correlated with physical and chemical characteristics of wetlands and shallow lakes, the 12 most common species were compared by single classification ANOVA. For each species, the mean chemical or physical variable was determined from the sites having that particular species. For instance, Chydorus brevilabris occurred in 29 ponds. The mean pH value for Chydorus brevilabris sites was calculated and then compared to the mean value for each of the other 12 common species. When the ANOVA was significant, all pair-wise comparisons were run to determine which pairs of species differed in specific physical or chemical factors. The significance level was corrected for using the conservative Bonferroni correction, whereby the computed \( p \)-value is multiplied by the number of comparisons to estimate the Bonferroni corrected \( p \)-value. Significant ANOVA results were plotted as mean (+/- 1 standard error) to present the data graphically.

The relationship between number of taxa and water body size was analyzed using simple linear regression. Both lake size and number of taxa were log-transformed (as in Dodson, 1992). The relationship between lake duration and number of taxa was analyzed using linear regression of the untransformed data.

Pair-wise associations of taxa

Species pairs were analyzed using a \( 2 \times 2 \) contingency table Chi-squared test of independence (Grieg-Smith, 1983). To meet standard requirements of the Chi-square test, we analyzed only those taxa present in at least 10 water bodies. A total of 12 taxa were common enough to meet the criterion, and 66 chi-square pair-wise tests were conducted. Positive or negative correlation between pairs of species was determined by inspection.

Multivariate analysis of taxa associations

We performed cluster analysis in order to distinguish between wetlands and shallow lakes, using presence-absence data for zooplankton taxa. Euclidean distances generated under the nearest neighbor option were used to construct a dendrogram (Fig. 2). The resulting dendrogram was analyzed visually for pattern of associations of taxa. Cluster analysis and dendrogram construction was accomplished with the aid of PC-ORD, CLUSTR Program\textregistered.

We performed a spatial autocorrelation analysis and semivariance analysis on our species richness data using GS+ (2000) to evaluate whether spatial autocorrelation was evident and whether there was directionality to the spatial autocorrelation present. Isotropic and anisotropic spatial autocorrelation analyses were performed on species richness using Moran’s I. In this analysis, all of the weights in the adjacency matrix (Sokal & Oden, 1978) are set to 1, i.e. the statistic is weighted by distance between sample points rather than by simple adjacency. An autocorrelogram was produced by calculating this statistic for a variety of lag distances (distance class averages from 16 to 161 miles).

Results

All identified crustacean and insect taxa are listed in Table 1. Many of the physical and chemical variables (Table 2) were highly correlated (Table 3). All ion concentrations were inversely correlated with latitude. Major ion concentrations (but not nitrogen and phosphorus) were directly correlated with conductivity. Water body size was significantly correlated only with chloride concentration. The strongest correlation was an inverse relationship between pH and latitude; pH was also correlated with alkalinity, calcium, chloride and nitrogen.

Number of Taxa

Geographic region and number of taxa

We detected 53 taxa (Table 1). The average number of taxa was 6.83 taxa per site. The average number of taxa per site, calculated for the sites in each of the three geographic regions (Fig. 1), did not differ significantly (one-way ANOVA, \( p > 0.05 \)). Latitude was not significantly correlated with species richness.

Physical and chemical variables and the number of taxa

Multiple regression analysis of species richness and the 12 physical and chemical variables shows significant inverse relationships with three closely-related measures of water chemistry. Two different procedures were used which arrived at two different models.
